slides.title: From Soft Lookup to Self-Attention
bullets: Recap from Week 1: Attention acts as a soft key-value lookup mechanism
Input sequence embeddings X in R^(N x d_model) represent sequence tokens
Self-attention enables tokens within the same sequence to attend to each other
Queries (Q), Keys (K), and Values (V) are generated from the same input sequence

figure.caption: Overview of Self-Attention Dataflow
steps: Queries Q, Keys K, Values V

slides.notes: In Week 1, we introduced attention conceptually as a database-like soft lookup where a query matches keys to compute a weighted sum of values. In self-attention, the queries, keys, and values all originate from the exact same sequence of input vectors. Every token in the sequence gets to look at every other token, producing a contextual representation that captures dependencies regardless of distance.

slides.title: Linear Projections for Queries, Keys, and Values
bullets: Project input representations X using three learnable weight matrices
W^Q in R^(d_model x d_k), W^K in R^(d_model x d_k), W^V in R^(d_model x d_v)
Query matrix Q = X W^Q with dimensions N x d_k
Key matrix K = X W^K with dimensions N x d_k
Value matrix V = X W^V with dimensions N x d_v
slides.notes: To allow the model to learn different interaction spaces, input embeddings X are projected into separate Query, Key, and Value spaces. We multiply X by three independent, learnable weight matrices W^Q, W^K, and W^V. The Query and Key projections share the dimension d_k because we must take dot products between them. The Value projection dimension d_v can differ, though in practice it often equals d_k.

slides.title: The Scaled Dot-Product Attention Formulation
bullets: Compute dot product similarity between queries and keys: Q K^T
Scale the raw dot product scores by 1 / sqrt(d_k)
Apply row-wise softmax to convert similarity scores into probabilities
Multiply softmax probabilities by values V to get context matrix Z
Equation: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V
slides.notes: This fundamental formula forms the heart of the Transformer architecture. We matrix-multiply Q by K transpose to get an N-by-N matrix of similarity scores. We divide these scores by the square root of d_k, pass each row through softmax to get normalized attention weights summing to 1, and finally compute a weighted sum over the Value vectors.

slides.title: Why Scale by the Square Root of Key Dimension?
bullets: High-dimensional vectors produce large dot products under independent components
If Q_i and K_i are independent zero-mean unit-variance random variables, Var(Q . K) = d_k
Large magnitude logits push the softmax function into regions with tiny gradients
Scaling by 1 / sqrt(d_k) controls the variance back to 1.0
Prevents vanishing gradients during backward propagation
slides.notes: Why do we scale by the square root of d_k instead of using unscaled dot products? As the key dimension d_k grows large, dot product magnitudes grow proportionally to d_k, making their variance equal to d_k under standard initialization. Large dot product values push the softmax function into regions where output gradients are extremely small, leading to vanishing gradients. Dividing by sqrt(d_k) stabilizes training.

slides.title: Matrix Form and Dimension Tracking
bullets: Input sequence matrix X has shape (N, d_model) where N is sequence length
Q and K have shape (N, d_k); Transposed K^T has shape (d_k, N)
Matrix product Q K^T has shape (N, N) representing all pair-wise attention scores
Softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) preserves (N, N) matrix dimensions
Multiplying by V with shape (N, d_v) yields output Z of shape (N, d_v)

figure.caption: Tensor Dimensions in Scaled Dot-Product Attention

slides.notes: Tracking tensor dimensions is critical for understanding and implementing self-attention in code. Notice how sequence length N dictates the inner dimensions of the score matrix (N x N), while key dimension d_k is contracted away during matrix multiplication. The final output has sequence length N and dimension d_v, matching the input length while enriching feature representations.

slides.title: Worked Example: Unmasked Scaled Dot-Product Step-by-Step
bullets: Let sequence length N = 2, key dimension d_k = 4, so sqrt(d_k) = 2.0
Dot product matrix Q K^T = [[2, 0], [0, 4]]
Scaled scores matrix (Q K^T / 2.0) = [[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 2.0]]
slides.notes: Let's walk through a numerical calculation step by step. With key dimension d_k = 4, our scaling factor sqrt(d_k) is 2. Matrix multiplying Q by K^T yields raw scores [[2, 0], [0, 4]]. Scaling by 2 gives [[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 2.0]]. Applying row-wise softmax converts row 1 [1.0, 0.0] to [0.731, 0.269] and row 2 [0.0, 2.0] to [0.119, 0.881].

slides.title: Checking Understanding: Scaling Factor Impact

quiz.question: If key dimension d_k increases from 16 to 64, by what factor should the raw dot products Q K^T be scaled before applying softmax?
quiz.explanation: The scaling factor is 1 / sqrt(d_k). For d_k = 64, sqrt(64) = 8, so the scaling factor is 1/8. Option A (1/4) incorrectly uses sqrt(16) or takes 16/64, while Option D (1/64) forgets the square root entirely.

slides.notes: Let's test our understanding of the scaling factor. Remember that we scale by the square root of d_k, not by d_k itself. For d_k = 64, the square root is 8, making the scale factor 1/8.

slides.title: The Purpose of Causal Masking in Decoder Layers
bullets: Autoregressive language models predict token i using only preceding tokens 1 to i - 1
Standard self-attention allows all tokens to attend to all other tokens bidirectionally
Unmasked self-attention in a decoder would leak future tokens during training
Causal masking prevents query position i from attending to key positions j > i
Ensures model predictions strictly depend on historical context
slides.notes: When training autoregressive Transformer models like decoders, we want the model to predict the next word given past context. However, self-attention allows every token to see every other token in the sequence. To prevent token i from looking ahead at future target tokens j > i, we apply a causal mask that zeroes out attention probabilities for all future positions.

slides.title: Constructing and Applying the Causal Mask
bullets: Create an upper triangular mask matrix where forbidden positions (j > i) are marked
Set forbidden positions to -infinity (or a large negative value like -1e9)
Add the mask matrix to scaled dot product scores prior to Softmax computation
Formula: Softmax( (Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) + Mask )
Since exp(-inf) = 0, softmax assigns exact 0.0 attention weight to future tokens

figure.caption: Additive Mask Matrix Structure for N = 3

slides.notes: We implement causal masking by adding an upper-triangular matrix containing negative infinity (-inf) values above the main diagonal to the scaled dot product scores before passing them to the softmax function. Because e raised to -inf equals 0, the softmax outputs exact zero attention weight for all future positions j > i.

slides.title: Worked Example: Masked Self-Attention Step-by-Step
bullets: Given sequence length N = 3 and scaled scores for Position 3: [0.5, 2.0, 2.0]
All three keys are valid for Position 3 under causal mask (j <= i: 1, 2, 3 <= 3)
Exponential terms for Position 3 raw scores: e^0.5 approx 1.65, e^2.0 approx 7.39, e^2.0 approx 7.39
Sum of exponentials = 1.65 + 7.39 + 7.39 = 16.43
Position 3 output is 0.10 * V_1 + 0.45 * V_2 + 0.45 * V_3

figure.caption: Step-by-Step Causal Masked Attention Scores & Weights

slides.notes: Let's examine how masked self-attention works across positions. Position 1 can only attend to itself, getting weight [1.00, 0.00, 0.00]. Position 2 attends to positions 1 and 2, yielding [0.50, 0.50, 0.00]. For Position 3, raw scores are [0.5, 2.0, 2.0]. Computing exponentials yields 1.65, 7.39, 7.39. Dividing by their sum 16.43 gives softmax weights approximately [0.10, 0.45, 0.45].

slides.title: Checking Understanding: Causal Masking Mechanics

quiz.question: Why is negative infinity (-inf) used in the additive attention mask instead of 0?
options: Because 0 added to logits would leave them unchanged, allowing future tokens to get non-zero softmax weight
Because softmax(0) equals infinity, which causes numerical underflow
Because negative infinity sets matrix values to zero prior to matrix multiplication
Because PyTorch does not support boolean masking during forward pass
quiz.explanation: Adding 0 to raw scores (logits) leaves them as-is, which would result in non-zero softmax probabilities e^score / sum. Adding -inf ensures exp(-inf) = 0, giving exact 0 softmax weight to future tokens. Option B is incorrect because exp(0) = 1, not infinity.

slides.notes: Understanding why we use -inf for masking is essential. An additive mask modifies logits before softmax. If we added 0, the logit would remain unchanged and receive positive softmax probability. Adding -inf ensures e^(-inf) = 0.

slides.title: Vectorized PyTorch Implementation
bullets: Implement scaled dot-product attention efficiently in PyTorch without python loops
Use torch.matmul for matrix multiplication across batch and sequence dimensions
Generate lower-triangular causal mask using torch.tril
Apply mask using tensor.masked_fill(mask == 0, float('-inf'))
Compute softmax along the last dimension: dim=-1

figure.caption: PyTorch Scaled Dot-Product Attention Function
figure.code:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def scaled_dot_product_attention(Q, K, V, mask=None):
    d_k = Q.size(-1)
    scores = torch.matmul(Q, K.transpose(-2, -1)) / torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(d_k, dtype=torch.float32))
    if mask is not None:
        scores = scores.masked_fill(mask == 0, float('-inf'))
    attn_weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1)
    output = torch.matmul(attn_weights, V)
    return output, attn_weights

slides.notes: Here is clean, vectorized PyTorch code for scaled dot-product attention. Notice how K is transposed across its last two dimensions with transpose(-2, -1). We calculate scores, apply masked_fill where mask is false/0, evaluate softmax along dim=-1, and multiply by V.

slides.title: Computational and Memory Complexity
bullets: Matrix multiplication Q K^T requires O(N^2 * d_k) operations per sequence
Attention weight matrix requires O(N^2) memory storage
Quadratic scaling with sequence length N creates a bottleneck for long contexts
Matrix multiplication with V requires O(N^2 * d_v) operations
Motivates linear attention models and FlashAttention implementations

figure.caption: Complexity Comparison of Sequence Layer Operations

slides.notes: Self-attention provides direct O(1) path length between any two tokens, enabling excellent long-range modeling. However, computing and storing the N-by-N attention matrix incurs O(N^2) time and memory complexity. For long sequences (e.g., N > 4090), this quadratic bottleneck becomes severe, driving the development of FlashAttention and linear attention variants.

slides.title: Summary: Scaled Dot-Product Self-Attention
bullets: Self-attention projects sequence inputs into Query, Key, and Value matrices
Raw similarity scores Q K^T measure alignment between queries and keys
Scaling by 1 / sqrt(d_k) prevents vanishing gradients caused by high-dimensional dot products
Causal masking adds -inf to future positions to preserve autoregressive ordering
Vectorized PyTorch implementation uses matmul, masked_fill, and row-wise softmax
slides.notes: To summarize, scaled dot-product attention transforms input sequences into contextual representations by comparing Queries and Keys, scaling by sqrt(d_k), masking future positions with -inf, and taking a weighted sum of Values. Mastering this single block is essential before we extend it to Multi-Head Attention in the next class.
